visits.text: The big day: swimming with dolphins. Wake 5-5:30am, departure from Albion at 6am, boarding at La Jetty Road in Black River at 6:45am. On the west coast, two species - the spinner dolphin, in large playful groups, and the bottlenose dolphin, more discreet. Boats cut the engine on approach, you enter the water gently. Favour Vitamin Sea or Dolswim: 8 people max, ethical approach. Avoid: boats that chase and encircle, it's become a real problem here. Count on 2,500 MUR/adult, 1,800 MUR/child with serious operators.

La Preneuse beach for recovery after the dolphins: white sand, calm lagoon, perfect for recovering from the 5am wake. The coral reef is 50 metres out. The casuarinas give shade all day, food trucks on weekends. Kids can sleep on the beach while parents read.

La Preneuse Martello Tower, British fortification from 1810 built to defend the Black River mouth against the French. Small interior museum (cannons, uniforms, battle plans), entrance 200 MUR, visit in 45 minutes. Panoramic view from the roof. Ideal for history-curious teenagers - big chunk of explanation on the Napoleonic Wars seen from the Indian Ocean.

Humpback whale outing departing from Black River. July is in the heart of the season (June to October): females come to give birth in Mauritian warm waters, barely 1 km from the west coast. Spectacle guaranteed 90% in this period - full breaches, tail slaps. Warning: swimming with whales is not authorised, boat observation only (at regulatory 100m). Longer outing than dolphins, 4-5h. Vitamin Sea offers a combo dolphins + whales + sperm whales over 5h, at 4,000 MUR/adult.

Casela Nature Park as an afternoon option (or a full day if you skip the whales), 10 minutes from Albion. 350 hectares, a mix of wildlife park (giraffes to feed, zebras, ostriches) and adventure park. For the 6-year-old: Pangia Kids Park (mini farm, merry-go-round, mini golf). For the teenager: a 400 m zip line or the 40 m canyon swing. These last two are reserved for ages 14 and over with parents. As for the big cats, the park offers a 'walk with lions' and a tiger drive-thru - questionable practices in terms of animal welfare, best avoided.

Black River Gorges National Park, less than an hour's drive from Albion, 6,754 hectares created in 1994, 2% of Mauritian territory. For a family with a 6-year-old, two simple options: the Macchabée Forest Walk (2.5 km, flat and shaded, 1.5 hours, starting from the Pétrin centre) or the Gorges Viewpoint by car plus a short trail (15 minutes' walk, spectacular view over the valley). Avoid the climb up Piton de la Petite Rivière Noire (828 m, the highest point) with a little one, it is too much. 9 endemic bird species can be seen: Mauritius fody, pink pigeon, Mauritius kestrel - patience and binoculars.

Grand Bassin (Ganga Talao), 3 minutes from Pétrin, crater lake sacred to the Mauritian Hindu community (52% of the population). 33-metre Shiva statue erected on the lake shore, one of the tallest in the world. Massive pilgrimage late February-early March (Maha Shivaratri, up to 500,000 faithful). In July, calm and majestic atmosphere. Modest dress required (shoulders and knees covered).

Chamarel and the Seven Coloured Earth, 30 minutes after leaving the park. An astonishing geological phenomenon: dunes of volcanic ash in 7 shades (red, brown, violet, green, blue, purple, yellow). Small, but definitely worth seeing once. On the same site, a view of the Chamarel waterfall (100 m drop) and an Aldabra tortoise park. Combined ticket 350 MUR per adult, free for under-3s.

Domaine de Bel Ombre, 2,500 preserved hectares on the wild south coast, more than an hour's drive from Albion. Far from the crowds, it is the closest thing to pre-tourism Mauritius. Activities: nature rides on horseback (from age 6, riding double with a guide) and 2-seater buggies on the estate's tracks (1.5 hours, 3,800 MUR per buggy).

Flic en Flac beach, 15 minutes south of Albion, 8 km of white sand, one of the largest on the island. An ideal lagoon for children: shallow for 200 metres, sandy bottom. Casuarinas for shade. The southern stretch (Wolmar) is wilder, the northern stretch livelier. A snack at Domino's Pizza or Chez Pepe for a cheap lunch.

activities.text: A nap on Albion beach after the dawn start. The public beach is small but deserted on weekdays, with direct access from the village. Albion lighthouse visible in the distance (built in 1910).

Creole dinner at Pavillon de Jade or Domaine Anna in Flic en Flac: grilled fish (captain or red snapper), sausage rougaille, homemade dessert. Mauritians also go there on Friday nights, sign that it's good. Count on 600-800 MUR per adult main course.

Buggy or electric eco-rider at Casela through the Yemen reserve (4,500 hectares, one of the largest private wild spaces on the island). Javan deer in herds (about 9,000 individuals), wild boars, mongooses. 2h ride, departures 9:15am and 2:45pm. Minimum age 16 to drive a buggy, so dad/mum at the wheel and passengers in back. The silent 4x4 eco-ride is open to the whole family (from 4 years).

Sunset at Tamarin on the surfers' beach, about twenty minutes' drive south of Albion. The best-known Mauritian waves are here: 1 m to 2 m in July, intermediate level. A guaranteed show, and surf school possible for the teenager (1,500 MUR for a 1.5-hour session). Le Dock beach bar 50 m away, mocktails and tapas.

Tasting break at Rhumerie de Chamarel for adults (distillery tour 1h, tasting of 5 agricultural rums at 350 MUR/person). L'Alchimiste restaurant on site, revisited Creole cuisine, colonial veranda atmosphere. Meal 1,200 MUR/adult, children's menu 450 MUR. Kids receive freshly pressed sugarcane juice during the tasting.
A picnic at the Pétrin Information Centre before the walk, or gâteaux piments from the food trucks at Plaine Champagne. Locals stop there on their way down from pilgrimages.

Discovery dive at Flic en Flac for the teen (from 8 years with PADI certified instructor). Several centres: Sun Divers, Exploration Sous-Marine. Baptism in pool then sea outing in the 5m range, view of the coral reef. Count on 2,800 MUR for baptism with photos. The 6-year-old can snorkel during this time.

Farewell dinner at La Pirogue or at Le Bistrot du Boucanier in Flic en Flac, last night before the all-inclusive at Le Morne. Creole-French fusion cuisine, terrace facing the sunset. Count on 1,500 MUR/adult. Good address for Mauritian seafood (prawns, lobsters, crabs).

places.name: Blue Bay

visits.text: First contact with the island: Blue Bay beach and its marine park, protected since 2004. Its electric-blue water gives the place its name. The coral reef starts almost within swimming distance of the public beach: pack fins, mask and snorkel, and the children can watch parrotfish and surgeonfish in 1 metre of water. Handy for a first afternoon without driving too far from the airport. Avoid the spot on Saturdays and Sundays, when it fills with Mauritian family picnics - friendly but noisy.

Peaceful swimming at Pointe d'Esny, right next to Blue Bay but far less crowded. White sand beach, shallow lagoon extending 200 metres offshore - ideal for the 6-year-old who can splash around without worry. A few casuarina trees provide shade in the afternoon. No street vendors here, you feel more at home than on a postcard beach.

Île aux Aigrettes, 850 metres offshore from Mahébourg: probably the most striking nature visit on the island for children. 26 hectares of coral limestone (so not volcanic like the rest of Mauritius) managed since 1986 by the Mauritius Wildlife Foundation. You walk among giant Aldabra tortoises weighing over 200 kg, some centenarians, reintroduced to replace the Mauritian tortoises extinct around 1735. Guided tour mandatory, 1h30 on the Dodo Trail. Book 2-3 days ahead at 631 2396, the 9:30am slots fill up fast. Price: around 1000 MUR adult, 500 MUR children 4-11 years.

The National History Museum in Mahébourg, housed in an 18th-century French colonial mansion. A room is devoted to the naval Battle of Grand Port (August 1810), the only French naval victory inscribed on the Arc de Triomphe in Paris. Teenagers are often hooked by the ship models and cannons. A small but well-made museum, free, perfect in the middle of the day when the heat is strong. Closed on Tuesdays.

The Dutch ruins of Vieux Grand Port, 10 minutes north of Mahébourg. This is where the Dutch first set foot in 1598 - the birthplace of the island's modern history. Modest ruins (foundations, tombs), but the panorama over the bay is superb and the site is deserted. A chance to explain to the kids that the dodo, exterminated here in less than a century, lived its final days in these forests.

La Vanille park in Rivière des Anguilles, half an hour's drive from Blue Bay, an almost guaranteed favourite with families with young children. 1,000 Aldabra giant tortoises roaming in semi-supervised freedom, 2,000 Nile crocodiles bred on site, and an insectarium that gives teenagers the shivers. The big show: crocodile feeding, every day except Monday and Friday at 11:30. Allow 2 to 3 hours on site. Decent restaurant on site if you want to carry on.

Rochester Falls in Souillac, about forty minutes' drive from Blue Bay, an unusual waterfall formed by rectangular basalt prisms sculpted by erosion. Modest height, 10 metres, but the geological effect is unique on the island. Access via a potholed track through the cane fields - a high-clearance car is better. Swimming is possible in the pool, provided it has not rained in the previous days (a common occurrence). Avoid after 4 pm, the surroundings empty quickly.

Gris-Gris, about forty minutes' drive from Blue Bay, a cliff pounded by the rollers of the wild south. There is no coral reef here, so the ocean hits the rock directly: waves explode 10 metres high on the 'Roche qui pleure', a limestone formation carved by salt. Swimming strictly forbidden, violent currents. Five minutes' walk from the car park, accessible to young children.

activities.text: Peaceful swimming at Pointe d'Esny, right next to Blue Bay but far less crowded. White sand beach, shallow lagoon extending 200 meters offshore - ideal for the 6-year-old who can splash around without worry. A few casuarina trees provide shade in the afternoon. No street vendors here, you feel more at home than on a postcard beach.

Glass-bottom boat in Blue Bay Marine Park. 30 minutes above the coral gardens: table coral, Neptune's brain coral, anemones, and with luck some green turtles. Perfect format for the 6-year-old who won't snorkel for long. Count on 800 MUR per adult, half-price for children. The boats leave from Blue Bay public beach, you can negotiate on site without trouble.

Mahébourg market on Monday morning, the day of the big fair, or Curepipe central market as an alternative, half an hour's drive from Blue Bay. You will find the fruits of the austral winter there, including Victoria pineapple. Try the chilli-tamarind fruit salad, strange but addictive. The children choose their fruit, and stallholders often offer a piece to taste - it is the custom.

Visit to Saint Aubin at La Flora to wrap up the southern day. 1819 colonial house, former sugar mill converted: they still produce agricultural rum and vanilla. Guided distillery tour (1h), tasting for adults, freshly pressed sugarcane juice for kids. The veranda restaurant serves authentic Creole cuisine - the octopus vindaye is worth it if you're not put off by octopus.

Snack in Souillac: the famous gâteaux piments and samosas at Gardénia, a local institution since the 1970s. It's touristy, but well done - and far more instructive about Mauritian street food than hotel demonstrations. Count on 80 MUR for a snack for four.

places.name: Cap Malheureux

visits.text: Île d'Ambre is reached by kayak from Rivière La Chaux, at the northeast tip. Allow 2 to 3 hours for an excursion through the mangrove, with native forest and ruins of an old colonial quarantine station on the island. Operators offer these guided trips. No postcard beach – raw, little-visited nature.

Roches Noires: Mauritius's northeast coast is the island's least touristy. Black basalt, rough sea, constant wind. Poste Lafayette is a wild beach with wind and few people. Not a calm swimming beach – a coast for watching the sea.

Notre-Dame Auxiliatrice Church at Cap Malheureux has a bright red roof that stands out against the sky and sea – it's the most photographed image of Mauritius. Across the water, on clear days, you see Coin de Mire distinctly. A five-minute stop is enough, but evening light is best.

activities.text: The northeast coast is raw Mauritius – no resort, no polished lagoon. A good half-day's drive on small coastal roads between fishing villages. Plan to buy fresh fish at one of the roadside markets late in the day.

map_keywords: Île d'Ambre kayak La Chaux River

visits.text: Grand Bassin – Ganga Talao in Creole – is a crater lake at 550 meters altitude surrounded by multicolored Hindu temples. A 33-meter statue of Shiva greets you at the entrance. It's the most important pilgrimage site in Mauritius for the Hindu community. In February-March, during Maha Shivaratri, hundreds of thousands of pilgrims walk barefoot from across the island – sometimes 40 kilometers on foot to reach the lake.

Black River Gorges National Park covers 6,574 hectares – it's the largest area of native forest still standing in Mauritius. The Macchabée trails cut through canopy forest with tree ferns and rare endemic fauna. Allow 3 to 5 hours depending on your pace. Pack water, closed-toe shoes, and sunscreen.

Plaine Champagne is a 700-meter-high plateau with moorland landscapes unlike anything else in Mauritius. Alexandra Falls plunges into the gorges from this plateau – the viewpoint over the falls and the forest below is worth the 20-minute stop.

Arrive at the Seven Coloured Earth right at opening at 8:30am. After 10am, tour buses roll in and it's over. These volcanic earth dunes owe their colors to basalt decomposing into clays: iron oxides give the red and brown, aluminum oxides the blue and purple. The phenomenon is real – the colors never mix, even after torrential rain.

Chamarel Falls drops nearly 100 meters – it's the island's highest waterfall. The viewpoint is accessible from the Seven Coloured Earth site. It's more impressive during the rainy season (December-March), but visible year-round.

Chamarel Rum Distillery is the only arabica coffee operation in Mauritius, grown on volcanic soil at 300 meters altitude. It also produces rum – white rum, aged rum, spiced rum. Plan for the tasting: it's included in the tour and the bottles aren't available everywhere.

activities.text: Physical day – arrive in Chamarel late afternoon and settle in. The village is quiet, accommodations often tucked deep in the greenery. Good evening to do nothing at all.

Ebony Forest is a private reserve of native ebony forest with 140 plant species. The trail climbs to Point Sublime – a plunging view over Le Morne and the entire west coast. Allow 1.5 hours round trip. It's one of the rare chances to see what Mauritius looked like before deforestation.

visits.text: Eureka has 109 doors – yes, 109. This 1830 Creole house in Moka is the largest on the island, built in the typical colonial Mascarene style: verandas on three sides, camphor wood, period furniture. Wander through the rooms, look at the yellowed photographs, then head down to the garden – it follows a river where you can swim.

Trou aux Cerfs is a volcanic crater 300 meters across and 85 meters deep right in the heart of Curepipe. A path circles it in less than a kilometer. On clear days, you get the central plateau mountain chain on one side – and sometimes both coasts of the island.

Curepipe is Mauritius's wettest town, perched at 550 meters altitude. Misty in the morning, cool (18-22°C), it has the atmosphere of a colonial mountain town – wooden houses, covered market, slow rhythm. Pack a light sweater for the evening.

Domaine des Aubineaux is a late-19th-century colonial house with Italian frescoes painted on the ceilings and intact period furniture. In the garden, a colophane tree is over 500 years old – one of the oldest trees on the island. Admission is often included in Tea Route combo tickets.

Bois Chéri has been producing tea since 1892 – it's the island's first and oldest plantation. Tour the factory to understand the transformation process from leaf to cup. Then head up to the panoramic restaurant: the view over the south coast on clear days is worth the trip alone. Try the vanilla tea and coconut tea – they're the house signatures. ⚠️ The factory only runs tours certain days of the week: check before you go.

Saint Aubin Estate: a sugar plantation since 1819, one of Mauritius's oldest. It's here that the island's first agricultural rum is produced. The Vanilla House walks you through the entire transformation chain – from the Vanilla planifolia orchid to the dried pod. Allow 1.5 hours to tour the estate.

activities.text: If you're there on a Thursday or Sunday, detour to the Quatre Bornes market – the island's big textile market. Hundreds of stalls selling clothes, sheets, shoes at rock-bottom prices. Not touristy at all: this is where Mauritians do their shopping.

This is a day for the palate. Flavored tea tastings at Bois Chéri, aged rum and cane punch at Saint Aubin, fresh vanilla scraped on the spot. Leave space in your luggage – the teas and rums from these estates aren't as easy to find elsewhere.

places.name: Grand Baie

visits.text: Trou aux Biches is the perfect choice for an easy start. The lagoon is protected by a coral reef - the water is flat, crystal-clear, and you can stand far from shore. Arrive mid-morning when the sunlight hits the white sand just right.

Mont Choisy is the longest beach in the north: nearly 2 km lined with shade-giving casuarina trees. Less crowded than Trou aux Biches on weekdays - a solid option if you're looking for some breathing room.

Cap Malheureux owes its name to the shipwrecks that littered this wind-exposed headland. The Notre-Dame Auxiliatrice church - red roof, white walls - is one of the most photographed in Mauritius. Facing it, Coin de Mire rises on the horizon about 18 km offshore.

Pereybère is a pocket-sized beach with a different feel from Grand Baie - more local, less touristy. Vendors selling gâteaux piments walk along the seafront in the late morning. It is a few minutes' drive from Cap Malheureux. Bain Boeuf lies on the coast between the two - a calm cove, almost free of tourists.

The Sir Seewoosagur Ramgoolam Botanical Garden in Pamplemousses is one of the oldest in the tropics - founded in 1770 under Pierre Poivre, administrator of the Îles de France. It's home to over 650 species including giant Victoria amazonica water lilies and talipot palms, which flower only once in 60 years before dying. Allow at least 1.5 hours.

L'Aventure du Sucre in Beau Plan is a museum housed in a 19th-century sugar factory. It tells the story of sugarcane - and of the slavery that made it possible. The period machinery is still in place. Allow 1 to 1.5 hours.
The Château de Labourdonnais in Mapou is a colonial mansion built in 1859. The estate includes an orchard of 70 fruit species and an artisanal rum distillery. The guided tour takes about 45 minutes.

activities.text: Snorkelling straight from the beach at Trou aux Biches - sea turtles regularly frequent this area. No boat needed. Bring your mask and snorkel if you have them; local operators rent gear on-site.

Sunset from La Cuvette, the small cove at Grand Baie. This is where locals gather at the end of the day - the vibe is local, the orientation due west. It's about 15 minutes on foot from Grand Baie town centre.

Option A - if you haven't done the catamaran yet: afternoon swim at Pereybère or Bain Boeuf, local atmosphere, no resort in sight. Option B - if you prefer to dedicate this entire day to the islets: catamaran excursion to Coin de Mire, Île Plate, and Îlot Gabriel (about 6 hours, lunch on board, snorkeling around Îlot Gabriel). If going this route, book the day before and depart in the morning directly from Grand Baie harbour - Cap Malheureux and Pereybère can be done in 1 hour the evening before.
Tasting of rum and artisanal jams at Château de Labourdonnais. The house-made flavoured rums use fruit from the orchard - it's a short but pleasant stop at the end of the tour.

places.name: Le Morne Brabant

visits.text: The Seven Coloured Earths of Chamarel are a geological curiosity formed by the decomposition of volcanic basalt into clays of different colours - ochre, brick red, violet, khaki green. The dunes are about 100 metres in diameter. What's remarkable is that the colours don't mix even in the rain. The visit takes 30 minutes.

Chamarel Falls plunge about a hundred metres into the gorge below. They're among the highest in Mauritius. The viewing platform is accessible from the Seven Coloured Earths entrance - both visits are done together.
The Rhumerie de Chamarel produces agricultural rums. Tour the plantations, follow the distillation process and finish with a tasting. Allow 1 hour.

Ebony Forest is a private reserve protecting a forest of endemic black ebony - a critically endangered species. The trail to Point Sublime (about 1 km return) opens onto a 180° view of Le Morne and the west coast. Leave early morning to catch the light.

Le Morne Brabant rises to 556 metres and has been UNESCO-listed since 2008 - not for its geology, but for what it represents: in the 18th and 19th centuries, fugitive slaves took refuge in its inaccessible caves. Legend has it that they threw themselves off the cliffs on the day of the abolition of slavery in 1835, believing the soldiers who came to announce it were there to arrest them. The guided ascent takes 3 to 4 hours return. A guide is mandatory to reach the summit - book the day before.

activities.text: Descent to Le Morne mid-afternoon - 15 minutes' drive from Chamarel. The beach at Le Morne opens onto a perfectly calm lagoon on the north side. Swimming, hammock, or simply watching Le Morne Brabant from the water.

Kitesurfing in the Le Morne lagoon - it's one of the world's most renowned spots. The southeast wind blows steadily from May to November, and the lagoon is shallow with no current. Operators offer beginner courses. If you don't kitesurf, watching the riders from the beach is already worth something.
Sunset facing Île aux Bénitiers from Le Morne beach - the islet silhouettes to the west, the sky turns orange then red. This is the last proper evening of the circuit. Take it in.

visits.text: At Gris-Gris, forget the lagoon. Here the ocean pounds straight onto the rock – no coral barrier to slow it down. Wind blows, waves explode on the black cliffs. You'd think you were in Brittany, not the tropics. 200 meters away, La Roche qui Pleure is a cliff where water constantly seeps through by filtration in the volcanic rock.

Rochester Falls is 4 kilometers from Souillac. What makes this waterfall unique are its perfectly geometric rectangular basalt columns – as if someone had stacked bricks of black rock. Swimming possible in the pool below. Take the path from the parking lot: 10 minutes on foot.

La Vanille Nature Park is home to Aldabra giant tortoises – some over 100 years old and 200 kilos. There are also Nile crocodiles and an insectarium. It's not a spectacular animal park, but the tortoises you can approach and touch are worth the trip, especially with children.

Bel Ombre is a former sugar estate converted in the southwest of the island, with preserved nature and hiking trails in the hills. Not essential, but if you pass through, the nature reserve adjoining the estate gives an idea of what Mauritius looked like before sugarcane.

The National History Museum in Mahébourg occupies an early-19th-century colonial house. It traces the Battle of Grand Port in 1810 – Napoleon's only naval victory against the British. The name "Grand Port" is engraved on the Arc de Triomphe in Paris, among the great battles of the Empire. Allow an hour. On Mondays, the Mahébourg market sets up in front: fruit, spices, crafts – arrive early.

Blue Bay is a protected marine park with one of the best-preserved coral reefs on the island. Snorkeling from the beach or glass-bottom boat excursion to see corals without getting wet. The water is shallow – 2 to 4 meters in places – making it one of the best snorkeling spots in Mauritius.
Pointe d'Esny is the beach next to Blue Bay, quieter, bordered by mangrove. A handful of small Creole houses, few people. If Blue Bay is crowded, retreat here.

Last morning swim at Trou aux Biches or Mont Choisy – the two finest beaches in the north, 10-15 minutes from Grand Baie. Trou aux Biches is livelier, Mont Choisy wilder. Choose according to your morning mood.

activities.text: Road day through the wild south. Take the coast, stop when you want – it's a day of mileage and discovery. Pack a picnic or eat at a small restaurant in Souillac: the village is calm, authentic, no tourists.

Mahébourg is an authentic fishing village with a waterfront where locals gather at day's end. No tourist commerce, no resort. A good evening to eat grilled fish at a small local restaurant and watch the sea.

Last hour of shopping before the airport: Chamarel rum, vanilla tea from Bois Chéri, market spices, scale models of traditional Mauritian boats. SSR Airport is about 1h15 via the highway from Grand Baie – don't leave too late.

visits.text: First day at Mont Choisy: adopt the beach of the same name, 3 km of white sand and casuarinas, one of the longest public beaches in the north. Flat lagoon, ideal swimming for children, regular sandy bottom. On weekends it's full of Mauritian picnics (improvised sega, curry pots), on weekdays you have the beach to yourself. Street vendors of ice cream and pineapple boy - pineapple peeled on the spot for 50 MUR, irresistible in the heat.

Cap Malheureux, 15 minutes north, and its famous Notre-Dame Auxiliatrice church with bright red roof built in 1938. Clear view of the northern islets (Coin de Mire, Île Plate, Île Ronde) that look set on the turquoise water. Few visitors during the week, end-of-the-world atmosphere. One of the most photographed spots on the island - and for once, it's deserved.

Grand Baie late afternoon, the main tourist village in the north. Lively waterfront, shops, ice cream parlours, henna tattoo artists for teenagers. Less tacky than they say, but clearly more commercial than the rest of the island. Those who hate noise will pass by; those who want a feet-in-the-sand dinner at sunset will be served (Le Capitaine, La Plage, La Sirène).

A catamaran day to the northern islets (Coin de Mire and Île Plate), departing from Grand Baie. Choose Ocean Cruises Mauritius (20 places maximum), much less crowded than the boats carrying 60 to 80 people. On the programme: sailing, two snorkelling stops and a barbecue lunch on board. Allow 2,800 MUR per adult, 1,400 MUR per child.

Château de Labourdonnais at Mapou, neoclassical mansion from 1859 surrounded by a 540-hectare fruit estate. Visit with audio guide in French, walk through the orchards (mangoes, lychees, citrus), agricultural rum distillery on site. Children love the tasting at the end (fresh fruit juices, homemade jams). La Table du Château restaurant for lunch, set menu at 850 MUR per adult, children's dish 350 MUR.

Eureka, the Creole house in Moka, about forty minutes' drive from Mont Choisy: 109 doors, 109 windows, it is the largest wooden colonial house still standing on the island, built in 1830. You visit rooms furnished in period style and have lunch in the tropical garden overlooking the waterfall in the ravine. A particularity: people here speak French-Creole with a drawling accent and take their time. A fun anecdote for teenagers: the kitchen, 'gîte aux nègres', is separated from the main house by a covered passage to keep the smoke out of the bedrooms.

Trou aux Cerfs in Curepipe, less than an hour's drive from Mont Choisy, a perfectly circular volcanic crater 350 metres across and 85 metres deep, dormant for 700,000 years. A concrete road runs around it: 1.2 km in 20 minutes, doable with a pushchair. 360° view over the central plateau and the Black River mountain range. Curepipe is often rainy, so bring a windcheater even in July.

Quiet day to create a buffer before moving to Albion. Pereybère beach in the morning: small sheltered cove between Grand Baie and Cap Malheureux, white sand, crystal-clear water, and above all - less crowded than Mont Choisy. The reef is 20 metres from shore. Snack on site for lunch, no need to move.

Anse la Raie late afternoon: long beach facing Coin de Mire, ideal for kitesurfing in the austral winter (June-September). Guaranteed visual spectacle even without practising: 30-40 colourful sails above the lagoon, you'd think you were at a competition. Kids love watching. Several schools give introductory courses from 12 years old, interesting for the teenager.
Île Plate (Flat Island) as an option, by speedboat, for its beach. The crossing can be rough - avoid it with a 6-year-old if the sea is bad. Ask the operator the day before.

activities.text: Snorkeling at La Cuvette, small public beach hidden between two hotels in Grand Baie. Reef 30 metres from shore, clownfish in anemones, sometimes an octopus. Much quieter than nearby Trou aux Biches. Bring your gear, no rental here.

Evening aperitif on the Banana Beach Club rooftop or at the Beach House in Grand Baie. Nice mocktails for kids, tuna tartare for adults, view of the sunset over the bay. Reasonable pricing (350 MUR cocktail, 800 MUR dish) for a place that could easily inflate prices.

Snorkelling in the lagoon shared by Île Plate and Île Gabriel, the classic stop on the northern islets catamaran trip. Clear, shallow water, corals, parrotfish, sergeant majors and butterflyfish. On the way, the boat sails along the cliffs of Coin de Mire, a nature reserve where landing is not allowed. Float vests provided for the children, masks and snorkels included in the price of the trip.

A break on the sand of Île Gabriel, next to Île Plate, where the northern catamarans stop for lunch. A small island covered in casuarinas, a white sand beach and a shallow lagoon between the two islets, perfect for the 6-year-old. Relaxed family atmosphere. Coin de Mire is admired from the boat: a nature reserve with sheer cliffs, where no one lands.

A stop in the historic village of Mahébourg, more than an hour's drive from Mont Choisy, with its fruit market and fresh spice stalls. Mauritian massala (a unique blend with turmeric, coriander and cumin), vanilla pods at 100 MUR each, vegetable achards in jars. Edible souvenirs without breaking the bank. Choose the stallholder who lets you smell before buying - the best sign of freshness.

Street food dinner at Trou aux Biches: vegetable or chicken curry roti at Chez Ram, takeaway to the beach for sunset. 60 MUR for stuffed roti, 30 MUR for alouda drink. More authentic and fresher than half the tourist restaurants in the area.

Local spa massage for parents, beach games for kids. Coco Spa in Grand Baie offers essential oil massages at 1,500 MUR per hour (3-4 times cheaper than in hotels) and watches children for 30 min in a free play area. Very good reviews, book the day before.

Shopping at La Croisette in Grand Baie: model ships (the famous handmade 'modèles réduits', from 800 MUR), embroidered cotton tablecloths, vanilla pods. Avoid the 'duty free' shops at the Caudan, prices doubled.

visits.text: Get to the Central Market by 7am – that's when the stalls overflow with spices, tropical fruits, and fresh street food. Try the dholl puri, a split-pea-stuffed flatbread that's been sold on Port Louis streets for generations. Mine frit, gâteau piment, bol renversé: the market delivers the best meal of the day, and the cheapest.

Aapravasi Ghat has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2006. This wharf is where, starting in 1834, the first indentured laborers from India landed to replace enslaved workers after abolition. Between 1834 and 1924, nearly 500,000 people passed through. Plan for 45 minutes – the site is small but heavy with history.

The Blue Penny Museum holds two of the world's rarest stamps: the One Penny and Two Pence from 1847, the first stamps issued in Mauritius. They're only displayed in dim light to prevent deterioration. The museum also traces the island's history from the Portuguese onward – allow an hour.

Chinatown spreads around Rue Royale – a few blocks of pagodas, grocery stores, and Cantonese restaurants that recall Mauritius's waves of Chinese immigration since the 19th century. Not a polished tourist quarter: a genuine neighborhood enclave, with its smells and corner shops.

activities.text: Caudan Waterfront occupies renovated colonial warehouses facing the harbor. It's the most open-air corner of Port Louis – a solid option for a shaded lunch before the afternoon heat.

Climb up to Fort Adelaide – La Citadelle – late in the day. Built by the British between 1834 and 1840, it overlooks the city from 100 meters up. Late afternoon light on the harbor and Port Louis rooftops is the best you'll get all day. Bring water: the walk up from the center is steep.

days_plan.itin_title: Mauritius in Depth: 15 Days from the Interior to the Coast

visits.text: Île aux Cerfs from Trou d'Eau Douce, 10 minutes by water taxi. 87 hectares of white sand, swimming-pool-coloured lagoon - if you go, do it early. Touristy, definitely really touristy, but genuinely beautiful: before 9am, the southeastern beaches are almost empty and it's sublime. After 11am, it's a parade of catamarans and the beach transforms into Marbella beach. Private water taxis negotiate at 350-400 MUR round trip without guide or barbecue, much cheaper than group excursions.

The Grande Rivière Sud-Est waterfall, accessible as an option from Île aux Cerfs or from Trou d'Eau Douce. 30 minutes by pirogue through the mangroves to the two falls about 30 metres high. The pirogue operators approach to within 5 metres of the water curtain, shower guaranteed. It's basic, but well placed in the programme.

Domaine de l'Étoile, 1,200 hectares of private reserve 30 minutes from Trou d'Eau Douce. This is where you schedule the family buggy: minimum age 16 to drive, so dad or mum at the wheel and teen + little one as passengers in the back of a 4-seater buggy. 2-hour course through valleys, rivers and indigenous forests, stop in a river halfway to cool off. Probably the finest buggy spot on the island, and far less industrial than Casela. Count on 4,500 MUR for a 4-seater buggy.

Bras d'Eau National Park, about twenty minutes' drive north of Trou d'Eau Douce, a free and little-visited alternative for a family walk in the forest. Marked trail of about 3 km around an old colonial reservoir, doable in 1 hour with children. The information centres at the entrance lend maps and give the day's advice.

Port Louis, the capital, 1 hour's drive away. Start with the Aapravasi Ghat, a UNESCO site since 2006: this is where more than 450,000 Indian indentured labourers landed between 1834 and 1920. Remains of the original steps and buildings, free museum. Five minutes further on, the central market bursts with colours and smells - go through the spice wing, where Mauritian curry costs half the Curepipe price.

The Sir Seewoosagur Ramgoolam Botanical Garden in Pamplemousses, less than an hour's drive from Trou d'Eau Douce, the oldest tropical garden in the southern hemisphere (1735). 37 hectares, more than 600 species including the famous giant Victoria amazonica water lilies, 2 metres across and strong enough to hold a child - for the photo only, nobody tries. An avenue of talipot palms that flower only once in 60 years before dying. Guided tour recommended, 200 MUR for two hours with a French-speaking guide.

The Caudan Waterfront, old colonial port converted into a shopping-restaurant zone. Not revolutionary, but ideal for lunch after the market: shaded terraces, view of the sailboats, choice of cuisines (Creole, Indian, Chinese - Mauritius sums up its diversity in 100 square metres). The Crystal Pavilion serves a bol renversé at 350 MUR that fills a family.

activities.text: Snorkeling in the Île aux Cerfs lagoon on the east side, where the reef is most alive. Lots of butterflyfish, sergeant majors, sometimes stingrays in the sandy areas. The water is warm (24°C in July), shallow for 100 metres - suitable for the 6-year-old with a float vest. Water taxis provide fins-mask-snorkel on request, 100 MUR rental.

Beach barbecue lunch 'feet in the sand' on the island, either by booking via a water taxi (grilled fish + salad package for 600 MUR/person), or bringing your own picnic. More authentic than catamaran buffets, which feel industrial and end up at 80 people per table.

Archery, horseback riding or zip-lining at Domaine de l'Étoile: the full range of outdoor activities on the island is concentrated here. Children from 6 years old can ride double with a guide on horseback (30-min pony ride, 800 MUR). The domain's advantage: you combine several activities on the same day with a single entrance ticket at 300 MUR/person, more economical than doing them separately elsewhere.

Sunset on Belle Mare beach, 15 minutes north. 8 km white sand beach, one of the island's longest, little frequented late in the day as hotels pull in their towels. Peaceful swimming, wind a bit stronger than at Trou d'Eau Douce. Small cocktail at the fishing village beach bar around 5:30pm.

A break at the Champ de Mars, the oldest racecourse in the southern hemisphere (1812). If you happen to be there on a race Saturday (late March to early December), entry is free and the atmosphere electric: 30,000 Mauritians in jeans and shirts cheer on their horse. Otherwise, enjoy the view of the Citadel and the skyline from the central lawn.

Snack at L'île Maurice - Le Vieux Conseil, a Creole café-pastry shop in the cobbled alley behind the town hall. Napolitaine (cake filled with guava jam), Mauritian mille-feuille, alouda (milk-vanilla-basil drink): the canonical sweet break for Mauritians on a shopping outing, at local prices (40 MUR for napolitaine).
